hook.text: Category 1 tears off shingles. Category 5 flattens neighborhoods. The scale measures devastation.

buildup.text: The Saffir-Simpson scale ranks hurricanes from 1 to 5 based on sustained wind speed.

discovery.text: Category 3 and above are called major hurricanes — winds exceed 178 km/h.

twist.text: Wind speed alone doesn't tell the full story. Storm surge and rainfall cause most deaths.

climax.text: Hurricane Katrina was only Category 3 at landfall but caused $125 billion in damage.

punchline.text: The number on the scale matters less than where the storm hits.

quiz.question: What does the Saffir-Simpson scale measure?

details.summary: The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale classifies hurricanes into five categories based on sustained wind speed, from Category 1 at 119 km/h to Category 5 at 252 km/h or higher. It does not account for rainfall, storm surge, or storm size, which often cause more damage than wind.
details.whyItMatters: The scale shapes evacuation decisions and public perception of danger. Its focus on wind alone can cause people to underestimate the flood and surge threat from lower-category storms.
takeaways: Category 5 storms have sustained winds of 252 km/h or higher
Storm surge and rainfall cause most hurricane deaths, not wind
A large Category 1 can cause more damage than a small Category 3

faq.question: Why doesn't the Saffir-Simpson scale include flooding?
faq.answer: It was designed in the 1970s purely as a wind damage scale. Storm surge, rainfall, and flooding depend on factors like storm size, speed, and local geography that the simple five-category wind framework does not capture.

faq.question: What is the most dangerous hurricane category?
faq.answer: Any hurricane can be lethal. Hurricane Harvey was a Category 4 at landfall but its catastrophic flooding came from stalling and dumping 1.5 meters of rain. Storm surge from even Category 1 storms has killed thousands historically.
